\mxunit{enrichment-lattice-paths-notes}{Paths, combinations and Pascal}
\mxsubtitle{High school · counting \textperiodcentered{} Lesson and method \textperiodcentered{} 05}

\begin{prerequisites}
Products, factorials and unordered choices.
\end{prerequisites}

\begin{keypoint}[Ideas and method]
A path from $(0,0)$ to (a,b), using only rightward or upward steps, has $a + b$ steps. Choosing the positions of the a horizontal steps gives $C(a+b,a)$ paths.

For $0 \leq  k \leq  n$, $C(n,k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$. The order of the chosen objects does not matter. Symmetry $C(n,k) = C(n,n-k)$ corresponds to choosing included or excluded objects.

Pascal’s identity $C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k)$ splits choices by whether one fixed object is included. Paths can also be classified by their last step.
\end{keypoint}

\begin{example}
From $(0,0)$ to $(3,2)$, there are $C(5,3) = 10$ paths. To pass through $(1,1)$, choose one of two paths to that point and one of three paths onward: $2 \times  3 = 6$ paths.
\end{example}

\begin{activity}[Explore]
Draw a small grid and write the number of arriving paths at each vertex. Add the values of its left and lower neighbours.
\end{activity}
